questions.question: If training compute is roughly fixed at C = 6ND, what happens when you increase model parameters N a lot without raising compute?
options: You must usually train on fewer tokens D
You automatically lower inference cost
You increase both N and D together for free
You remove the irreducible loss term E
questions.explanation: With compute budget held fixed, parameters and tokens trade off against each other. Pushing N upward means D has to come down, which is exactly the tension the scaling-laws lesson analyzes.

questions.question: Why can benchmark abilities appear to “emerge” suddenly even when the underlying model improves smoothly?
options: Because transformers only learn after 1 trillion tokens
Because exact-match or thresholded metrics can hide gradual logit improvements
Because scaling laws stop applying beyond 10B parameters
Because post-training destroys smooth pretraining trends
questions.explanation: The lesson notes that discontinuous scoring rules can turn smooth changes in probability into abrupt-looking jumps in accuracy. That is why continuous metrics like cross-entropy are considered more reliable for forecasting.

questions.question: What token-to-parameter ratio did Hoffmann et al. find to be compute-optimal for pretraining?
options: About 2 tokens per parameter
About 20 tokens per parameter
About 200 tokens per parameter
About 2,000 tokens per parameter
questions.explanation: Chinchilla showed that the compute-optimal frontier is near D/N ≈ 20 rather than the much lower ratio used by GPT-3. The lesson uses that result to explain why GPT-3 was undertrained for its size.

questions.question: Why does the lesson say 2026 systems often over-train smaller models past Chinchilla-optimal?
options: Because training FLOPs dominate total cost forever
Because smaller models cannot use post-training
Because inference cost matters more for heavily deployed models, so longer training can be worth it
Because over-training eliminates the need for data curation
questions.explanation: Chinchilla optimizes loss per training FLOP, but production systems often care more about serving cost than one-time training cost. Training a smaller model on many more tokens can keep quality high while greatly reducing latency and inference spend.

questions.question: In the Hoffmann scaling-law equation L(N, D) = A / N^α + B / D^β + E, what does E represent?
options: The optimizer learning rate
The irreducible loss floor of the data distribution
The embedding-parameter penalty
The number of epochs needed for convergence
questions.explanation: E is the asymptotic floor you cannot beat just by scaling parameters or tokens. The lesson describes it as the irreducible loss ceiling or entropy of the data itself.
